title: perf: Add fast path for `Version` to `Version` comparison by skipping `_key` property
head: 659955c8a0f6025b4dd27dd0a4bce7e640b40bfe

families.why: Very short release tuples (1‑element) make tuple comparison extremely cheap, so the extra isinstance checks added in the new comparison overrides dominate the runtime. The old _BaseVersion.__lt__ performed a single isinstance check and a property access; the new version does two isinstance checks and explicit cache initialisation on every comparison.
families.size_meaning: Number of dot‑separated numeric segments in the release part (n). Cost grows with n because tuple comparison is O(n), but for n=1 the constant‑time overhead dominates.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Build a simple release version like '1.2.3' with n segments
    seg = '.'.join('1' for _ in range(n))
    return [[seg]]

families.why: The new version lazily builds the comparison key (_cmpkey) on the first comparison of each Version object. When many distinct Version objects are each compared only once (e.g., pairwise adjacent comparisons of a long list of unique versions), the new code pays the _cmpkey construction cost twice per comparison (once for each operand) while the original version may have cached the key earlier (e.g., in __init__ or via a property). This extra work makes the new version slower for workloads that create many unique versions and compare each only once.
families.size_meaning: n = number of distinct version strings; the benchmark will create n Version objects and perform n‑1 pairwise comparisons, each operand seeing its first comparison.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Produce n distinct simple version strings like '1.0.0', '1.0.1', …
    # Each element of the returned list is a single‑argument list for Version(...).
    return [[f"1.0.{i}"] for i in range(n)]

families.why: The new __lt__/__eq__ implementations add an extra isinstance(other, Version) check before falling back to the base class. When a Version instance is compared to a non‑Version object (e.g. int, str, None) the head version performs two isinstance checks instead of one, making the comparison slower.
families.size_meaning: number of dot‑separated release segments in the version string; larger n makes the version string longer but the slowdown is dominated by the extra type check, so cost grows only modestly with n
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Generate a simple dotted version like "1.2.3..." with n segments.
    segs = '.'.join(str(i) for i in range(1, n + 1))
    return [[segs]]

families.why: Pre‑release segment adds a (letter, number) tuple to the comparison key. Making the numeric part large (many digits) does not change tuple length but makes integer comparison a bit slower; the constant overhead of the new double‑isinstance check still dominates for small tuples.
families.size_meaning: Number of digits in the pre‑release number (n).
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # version like '1.0a' followed by n‑digit number
    num = '9' * n
    return [[f'1.0a{num}']]

families.why: The new comparison operators first test `isinstance(other, Version)` and then fall back to `super().__lt__(other)`, which repeats an `isinstance(other, _BaseVersion)` check. The old code performed only the single `_BaseVersion` check. When a workload repeatedly compares Version objects with instances of a different `_BaseVersion` subclass (a realistic scenario in downstream libraries that subclass `_BaseVersion`), the extra type check adds measurable overhead per comparison.
families.size_meaning: n = number of repeated comparisons between a Version instance and a non‑Version `_BaseVersion` subclass instance.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Produce a single simple version string; the benchmark will create one Version
    # and one dummy `_BaseVersion` subclass instance and compare them n times.
    # The argument list contains the version string for the Version constructor.
    return [["1.0.0"] for _ in range(n)]

families.family: comparison with non-Version objects (complex local part)
families.why: Same extra isinstance overhead as the simple family, but the version strings contain a large local‑version component (many dot/underscore separated segments). The head version still pays the extra type check while also paying the (identical) key‑construction cost, so the relative slowdown is more visible for larger n.
families.size_meaning: number of segments in the local version part; each segment adds a dot/underscore separated token, increasing key construction work
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Build a version with a large local part: "1.0+local.seg1.seg2....segN"
    local_segments = '.'.join(f'seg{i}' for i in range(1, n + 1))
    version_str = f'1.0+{local_segments}'
    return [[version_str]]

families.family: Invalid version strings that nevertheless contain indicator characters (e.g. a trailing dot followed by a letter). The fast‑path still does the full scan before the regex fails.
families.why: Even though the version is invalid, the extra disjoint check runs; the regex then fails. This is the single allowed invalid family.
families.size_meaning: Number of dotted segments before the malformed tail.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # "1." repeated n times then an alphabetic tail – not a valid PEP‑440 version
    version = "1." * n + "x"
    return [(version,)]

families.family: invalid strings that look simple (only digits and dots) but contain a non‑numeric segment, e.g. "1.2.x"
families.why: The indicator set is disjoint, so the fast path is entered. The code then executes `tuple(map(int, version.strip().split('.')))`, which raises `ValueError` on the bad segment; the exception is caught and re‑raised as `InvalidVersion`. Exception handling is considerably slower than the original regex‑only failure path.
families.size_meaning: n = number of leading numeric segments before the bad segment; larger n makes the split and the failed `int` conversion traverse more items before the exception.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # build "1.1.1....1.x" with n numeric parts then a non‑numeric "x"
    good = ".".join("1" for _ in range(n))
    version = f"{good}.x"
    return [[version]]

families.family: Single repeated segment "999." n times plus prerelease c5
families.why: The fast‑path’s `isdisjoint` test iterates over every character. For a long dotted release the string length grows with n, so the extra scan adds linear overhead before the (already linear) regex match.
families.size_meaning: Number of dotted release segments (plus the trailing pre‑release).
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    release = ".".join(["999"] * n)
    version = f"{release}c5"
    return [(version,)]

families.family: Versions with many release segments and a pre‑release suffix (e.g. "1.2.3…a1"). The fast‑path scans the whole string looking for indicator characters, finds the “a”, then falls back to the regex parser – an extra O(n) pass over the input.
families.why: The fast‑path’s `isdisjoint` test iterates over every character. For a long dotted release the string length grows with n, so the extra scan adds linear overhead before the (already linear) regex match.
families.size_meaning: Number of dotted release segments (plus the trailing pre‑release).
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Build "1.2.3…n" then add a pre‑release marker "a1"
    release = ".".join(str(i) for i in range(1, n + 1))
    version = f"{release}a1"
    return [(version,)]
